stories.title: The Montreal Cognitive Assessment in Spanish-speaking countries in Latin America and the Caribbean: a systematic review
stories.description: The number of people living with dementia is increasing worldwide, with a particularly fast increase in low- and middle-income regions such as Latin America and the Caribbean. The Montreal Cognitive Assessment is widely used for cognitive screening in Spanish-speaking populations, but its consistent application across the region is uncertain due to cultural and linguistic diversity, lower educational attainment, and socioeconomic disparities. We conducted a systematic review of studies published up to 10 June 2024 that reported on the validation or cultural adaptation of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment for Spanish-speaking populations. Searches were performed in PsycInfo, PubMed, Scopus, EMBASE, Web of Science, LILACS, SciELO, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar. Inclusion criteria required studies in English or Spanish involving Spanish-speaking participants. Standard procedures were conducted for screening studies, extracting data, and assessing methodological quality. The study protocol was registered in the PROSPERO systematic review registry (Registration: CRD42023465794). Here, we show that from the 13 studies that met the eligibility criteria, most studies reported limited cultural or linguistic adaptation of the tool. Only two studies describe substantial modifications to the original version. Assessment using cultural and translation reporting checklists reveals that critical steps, such as professional translation, pilot testing, and input from local healthcare professionals, are often underreported. This review indicates that proper adaptation of cognitive screening tools requires attention to language, culture, and education level. Improving reporting practices and standardizing the adaptation processes could enhance the validity of cognitive assessments across Spanish-speaking populations in Latin America and the Caribbean. Dementia is becoming more common, especially in parts of the world with fewer resources, like Latin America and the Caribbean. Medical providers often use a tool called the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) to help detect early signs of dementia. However, this test may not work the same for everyone, especially in areas with different languages, cultures, and education levels. In this study, we looked at how this test has been adapted for Spanish-speaking people in those regions. We reviewed published research to see if the test was properly translated and adjusted for local needs. We found that most versions of the test were not fully adapted. This means the results may not always be reliable. Better translation and adaptation could help people get more accurate diagnoses in the future. Bustamante-Paytan et al. examine how the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) is adapted and validated in Spanish-speaking Latin American and Caribbean countries. They highlight the need for culturally and educationally sensitive tools to ensure equitable and accurate dementia screening across the region.
